chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
title: Writing "Traffic Jam" for Artie Shaw
summary: Shaw pressed McRae for a closing theme and McRae stalled with eight bars, which became "Traffic Jam".

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

MR. WELBURN: This is Huntington and Massachusetts Avenue.

Yeah. That's where the -- you know, where the Boston Pop up there. Now they got an underpass. Massachusetts Avenue ... it's a (Inaudible) building, (Inaudible) Traffic Jam. We had rehearsal and Boston Pop was breaking one day. Man, you couldn't get across the street nowhere. People come out all out in the street. I said, "This is a traffic jam." So Artie said, "When you're gonna write for me?" I say, "I gotta think first." And always would show him a piece of paper about like eight bars, you know. And that would make him mad. He say, "Where's the arrangement?" I say, "There it is right there. That's your next hit. I'm going to write the next hit for you." Artie Shaw was funny. It would make him (Inaudible). And Georgie Auld say, "Man, you're

the only musician I've ever known to get along with Artie Shaw. Man, he's something else."
And every time I -- He say write something for me, I say to myself, "Here it is right here."
"Write me something because I'm gonna be coming (inaudible) -- I'm going to be broadcasting for Back Bay in Boston coast to coast. You gotta write me something like yall got."
"I need a thing to go off the air with."
I say, "I gotcha. I'll write it for you over the weekend. I'm going to New York."
So I came back -- so they're rehearsing that Thursday -- Friday. He say, "Where's it? You got it?"
"Right here. There it is. Eight bars."
He say, "What is that, eight bars?"
I say, "When I come back, I'll bring it back," you know. I say, "Come down on the weekend."
